title: Usage unit framing cheat sheet
content:
Purpose
---
Quick internal reference for GTM and sales: how we present usage units, why tokens (vs. requests/seat), simple tiering templates, and guardrails for discounts and commercial negotiations. This is a compact cheat sheet — use for decks, SDR/Sales talk tracks, and pricing experiments.

Problem we solve with metric framing
---
- Customers want a single, predictable metric that maps to engineering cost drivers (GPU cycles + memory pressure) and product value (length and complexity of responses).
- Simple counts like ‘requests’ or ‘seats’ break down quickly: two requests can have wildly different cost profiles if one is a 4k-token summary and the other a 32-token fill-in-the-blank.
- Tokens align with tokenization and model execution costs; they generalize across text generation, chat, and embeddings with sensible conversion factors.

Why token-first pricing (concise framing for sales)
---
Elevator: "We price by the unit that actually drives compute — tokens. That means your bill tracks model work (length and complexity of responses) instead of arbitrary request counts. So you only pay for what the model does."
Key talking points:
- Direct cost alignment: tokens map to RSU on the runtime (KV cache size, attention compute).
- Predictable scaling: token volume grows linearly with user-visible activity patterns (average response length, re-rate).
- Cross-model comparability: tokens let us show equivalent costs across model sizes/quantizations by providing normalized token multipliers.
- Customer education: provide simple conversions (e.g., typical summary = ~250 tokens) so non-technical buyers can estimate usage.

Common objections + rebuttals
---
- “Tokens feel technical / hard to explain to product managers.” -> "We provide a short cheatsheet and sample mappings to UX actions (search, summarize, chat turn). We also offer a dashboard with token-per-route breakdown so finance/product can see real usage patterns."
- “OpenAI/Competitor uses different metrics / pricing.” -> "We show a conversion table and emphasize that tokens are the de-facto system metric under the hood; our pricing is transparent and we publish examples to demonstrate parity."
- “We care about concurrency/throughput not tokens.” -> "Tokens drive throughput costs too. For high-concurrency customers we offer Dedicated capacity (fixed-cost) or hybrid commits that convert tokens into reserved throughput at a discount."

Tiering templates (suggested names + target customers)
---
- Developer / Starter (self-serve): 0–100M tokens/month. Low-touch, API-first, standard models. Good for prototypes and early product-market fit.
- Growth / Scale: 100M–1B tokens/month. Preferred pricing, higher throughput limits, basic SLAs, SRE handoff for onboarding.
- Enterprise / Dedicated: 1B+ tokens/month or reserved GPU capacity. Negotiated pricing, long-term commits, on-prem/VPC options, compliance add-ons.
- Add-on units: embeddings units measured with a conversion factor (e.g., 1 embedding request = 128 tokens equivalent), private deployments (flat platform fee), premium retention/observability.

Discounting guardrails (sales guidance)
---
Principles: preserve unit economics, reward committed volume and term length, avoid ad-hoc seat-style discounts.
- Commit tiers: define clear thresholds (e.g., 100M, 500M, 1B). Discounts increase at predictable bands.
- Minimum ARR for custom SLAs: require >= $X (sales will substitute X) ARR for SLA/enterprise concessions.
- Time-bound promos: avoid permanent list price changes. Use limited-time onboarding credits or accelerated overage protection for first 3 months.
- No open-ended % discounts tied to feature parity; require reciprocal vendor commitments (referrals, co-marketing, case study).
- Hybrid offers: combine token discounts with reserved throughput credits for latency-sensitive customers. Example: 20% token discount + 50% reserved throughput uplift for 12-month commit.

Commercial examples (simple, shareable)
---
- Small SaaS prototype: Starter — pay-as-you-go @ $0.00002 / token for generation; estimated 2M tokens/mo -> ~$40/mo.
- Mid-market customer: Growth — 300M tokens/month commit at $0.000012/token (40% off list) with 6-month ramp and dedicated onboarding.
- Enterprise: 2B token annual commit -> negotiate blended price + Dedicated capacity add-on. Include fallback model policy and 99.9 SLA.

How to translate product features into token estimates (cheat conversion table)
---
- Short chat turn (user prompt ~20 tokens, model response ~80 tokens) ≈ 100 tokens/turn.
- Long-form summarization of a 3‑page doc ≈ 400–800 tokens. Use sample prompts to educate buyers.
- Embedding: normalize to token-equivalent where 1 standard embedding request = 128 token-equivalents (customer-visible label: "embedding units").
- Reranking/batch use: expose batch-multipliers in console to show per-item cost.

Competitive positioning notes (quick competitor bullets)
---
- OpenAI: familiar token model; our angle is production economics + observability + deployment modes (Dedicated/Private). Emphasize latency SLOs and unit-economics tooling that lowers effective token cost (caching, batching).
- Anthropic/Cohere: compete on model quality and research PR. Highlight Redwood’s operational controls (rollouts, A/B, policy fallbacks) that reduce downtime/regressions for product teams.
- Managed inference vendors/HF: emphasize our turnkey Dedicated and Private options with platform-grade SLAs and routing policies.

Sales playbook snippets (short scripts)
---
- SDR outbound: "Many teams we talk to underbudget because they count requests, not words. We price by tokens (we can show a 1‑page mapping from product actions -> tokens). Would you like a 2-minute example for your product?"
- AE discovery: "Walk me through a typical user flow — how long are generated responses, how often do you call the model? I can show a quick estimate and a low-risk starter plan."
- Procurement pushback: "If you’re worried about variability, we can structure a blended commit — part reserved throughput for predictable latency and part variable tokens for bursty usage."

Operational/Console expectations to communicate to customers
---
- Token-level reporting per route (required).
- Forecasting tool: simple projection using rolling 30-day tokens with alerting for % deviation.
- Cost optimization suggestions surfaced in console (char/response length triggers, batching recommendations, model/quantization hints).

Open questions / experiments to run (A/B ideas)
---
- Test: list price vs. anchored per-token with ‘‘starter credits’’ — which converts more self-serve signups?
- Bundling experiment: small embedding bundle included in Growth tier vs add-on at checkout.
- Sales incentive: measure win rate change when offering a hybrid commit (reserved throughput + token discount) vs token-only discount.

Notes to content/marketing: example artifacts to ship with pricing
---
- One-pager: "How to estimate your tokens" (with 5 product archetypes and token ranges).
- Calculator: simple web tool that maps user flows to token/day and to expected monthly cost.
- Sales cheat: short rebuttal card covering the three top token objections.

Quick reminders for negotiators (internal)
---
- Always tie discounts to commitments (volume, term, or proof-of-value activities).
- Preserve market anchor: if you give deep discounts beneath list, ensure registration in commercial governance and time-limited clauses.
- Use add-ons to preserve unit economics (dedicated capacity, observability).

Appendix: sample estimation worksheet (to paste into sales emails)
---
- Step 1: Count: average response length in tokens, average prompts/turns per active user/day.
- Step 2: Multiply: tokens/turn * turns/user/day * active users * 30 -> monthly tokens.
- Step 3: Price: apply tier price per token and show baseline vs. 20% uplift scenarios.

End — keep this short card in your deck and adapt language for customer sophistication.

Unresolved items / follow-ups
---
- Finalize the canonical embedding-to-token equivalency (ops/infra to confirm exact multiplier).
- Quantify minimum ARR threshold for enterprise SLA concessions (revOps to define $X).
- Run A/B pricing experiments in Q1 to validate starter credit designs.
